deep_why: The core task is ensuring a language model's response remains defensible when deployed—meeting privacy, safety, and accuracy standards under real constraints. The underlying principle is that guard-rails compound: a single safeguard (role prompt, format constraint, output filter) catches some failures, but combining them in sequence catches failures the earlier guards miss, because each guard addresses a different failure mode (leaking identity, misunderstanding the task, hallucinating a claim). This principle holds because different failure modes arise from different causes—one guard alone cannot catch everything, but each guard removes a distinct set of problems. By flowing a response through multiple gates before deployment, practitioners can measure what fraction still fails the toughest tests (red-team probes), then decide whether the residual risk is acceptable. This method lets teams take accountability for what ships: they have clear metrics, not hope.

The core thing tracked is how the Web's success metrics shift from satisfying a single isolated query to sustaining a person's long-term sense of value from a service. The underlying principle is that optimization shapes design: if you measure only whether a user found a specific document today, you optimize for document ranking; but if you measure whether that user returns next month and remains engaged, you optimize for relationship and surprise. This principle applies because user behavior changes when incentives change—creators, platforms, and services all respond by reorganizing toward what is measured. The transition from retrieval-centric to experience-centric metrics has redirected how the Web's biggest systems are built, from libraries focused on precision to platforms focused on habit formation. Understanding this evolution reveals why today's AI-augmented services emphasize dialogue and adaptation over one-shot answers.

The core problem is ranking visual search results by semantic relevance rather than surface appearance—distinguishing a visually similar but functionally wrong product from the right one. The underlying principle is that semantic meaning lives in hierarchies: a red glove and a red ball both share 'redness', but only the glove shares 'hand-covering purpose'. Learning that hierarchy first (category: headwear, footwear, glove) before learning fine details lets a model suppress irrelevant matches at multiple depths. This principle applies because real product catalogs are naturally structured—items cluster by function before clustering by appearance. By training in stages from coarse (proto-align to category, cross-view to robustness, then product-level detail), the model builds trustworthy intermediate checkpoints instead of trying to leap from pixels to distinctions. This staged approach reduces the chance of confusing two products that happen to share surface similarity but solve different problems.

The core thing being detected is collusive spam—groups that act together to amplify each other's fake signals. The underlying principle is that group behavior leaves fingerprints that individual behavior does not: if five accounts all review the same product within an hour, the timing co-occurrence itself is a strong signal, independent of whether each review individually looks authentic. This principle applies because groups are constrained by logistics and coordination; the pressure to act together creates temporal and relational patterns that a solo spammer cannot fake. By treating spam detection as a set-level problem—scoring groups rather than individuals—the method captures these collective signatures. This lets teams identify collusion that would slip past individual account scrutiny, because the 'conspiracy' signal lives in the group structure, not the text.

The core task is defending a federated knowledge graph system against an attacker who corrupts data on their local machine before shipping it to the shared model. The underlying principle is that poisoned data corrupts the learned representations in ways that spread: if one client injects bad information about, say, a person's relationships, the system learns wrong associations that then mislead all downstream tasks. Detection works by asking: are this client's contributed representations statistically like the others? If they are outliers—unusually sparse or dense compared to their peers—that signals tampering. This principle applies because honest data, even when diverse, usually clusters within a normal range of density in the learned space, while poisoned data often creates degenerate or extremely distorted patterns. Flagging and excluding anomalous clients before they corrupt the shared model preserves the integrity of the collaborative system.

The core problem is making recommendation systems robust when the patterns they learned during training no longer apply in the real world—for example, a recommendation engine trained on academic papers may see user preferences shift when users encounter a new topic. The underlying principle is that user interests have hierarchy: a person interested in 'reinforcement learning' nests under 'machine learning', which nests under 'computer science'. This hierarchy is real in the structure of knowledge and human curiosity. Hyperbolic geometry—which naturally encodes hierarchies with more space—lets the system represent these nestings explicitly, so it can separate true user interests (the stable hierarchy) from spurious correlations (surface patterns that don't generalize). Disentangling what is fundamental interest from what is context-dependent lets the model generalize when the world shifts.

The core challenge is answering a question by retrieving the right facts from a knowledge graph and chaining them into valid reasoning steps. The underlying principle is that small models are bottlenecks—they cannot hold complex reasoning in working memory the way large models can, so they need the reasoning organized outside themselves in the prompt. If you retrieve a dozen facts and dump them raw into the prompt, the small model gets lost; but if you organize those facts into 'answer-centered reasoning paths'—chains of logic that flow toward the answer—you give the model a scaffolding to follow. This principle applies because reasoning is sequential: fact A leads to fact B leads to fact C leads to the answer. By explicitly ordering retrieval this way and training the model to recognize which relations matter at each step, the method turns a haystack problem into a trail problem. Small models can follow trails even when they cannot find needles alone.

The core task is spotting fake news when the news originates from a previously unseen context—say, a new geopolitical crisis—with little labeled training data from that context. The underlying principle is that a large language model can extract high-level meaning (what is actually being claimed, what emotional tone is used) far better than hand-crafted features, because large models have learned richer language understanding from diverse text. However, meaning alone is insufficient; you also need to know whether this particular user typically shares misinformation, and whether this behavior is new for them. By combining semantic features from the large model with user-engagement history, and treating user behavior as domain-aware—learning what is typical in one domain versus another—the system can flag anomalies even when the news topic is fresh. The principle holds because misinformation detection is as much about behavioral anomaly as content: a user who suddenly shifts from sharing local news to conspiracy theories is more suspicious than their usual pattern.

The core thing being measured is whether a domain implements foundational security practices—whether it has certificates installed, whether DNS is hardened, whether it publishes security policies. The underlying principle is that security failures cluster when basic practices are skipped: if a domain does not implement one common measure, the odds it skips several others rise sharply. This is because security is economically motivated—a domain operator who invests in one safeguard has the incentive structure and expertise to adopt others, while one who skips all of them signals carelessness. By checking multiple foundational measures across many domains, the survey reveals these clusters. This lets stakeholders identify high-risk pockets of the Internet and understand whether security adoption is systematic or sporadic. The metric itself drives awareness: making the gaps visible is often the first step toward remediation.

The core challenge is determining whether a multimodal claim is false because the image is altered, because the text is wrong, or because they contradict each other—and realizing that existing detection methods miss many of these cases because they lump all falsehood together. The underlying principle is that falsehood has orthogonal dimensions: image authenticity, text authenticity, and cross-modal consistency are independent properties that can each fail alone or together. By treating the problem as an eight-way classification—all combinations of true/false image, true/false text, and matching/mismatched cross-modal meaning—the method forces clarity. Each case has a different upstream cause and a different remediation. This principle applies because exhaustive enumeration prevents blind spots: if you do not explicitly name all cases, your method will fail on some. By making the problem mutually exclusive and exhaustive, a detector can be held accountable for each region of the space.

The core task is predicting sentiment about a specific aspect (e.g., 'the battery') when the model is tempted to rely on shortcuts—like assuming all comments mentioning 'battery' in a certain context are negative, regardless of the actual claim. The underlying principle is that correlation and causation diverge: a spurious correlation (surface pattern and label happen to co-occur in training) is broken by changing just that surface pattern, while a causal feature (the actual meaning of the aspect in context) persists under change. By generating counterfactual examples—versions of a sentence where you swap the aspect or the context while preserving the true causal relationship—you force the model to learn what actually matters rather than memorize co-occurrences. This principle applies because a causal feature must generalize beyond the original distribution: if the model truly learned 'battery discharge complaints are negative', it should stay negative even when the surface words change. Testing this via counterfactual robustness prevents shortcuts.

The core problem is finding the cheapest set of nodes to remove from a network to break its largest connected cluster—a critical problem because in misinformation networks, cutting off information spread at the source is far cheaper than addressing every user it infects. The underlying principle is that reverse thinking works: instead of asking 'which nodes should I remove', ask 'if I start with these nodes gone, which would I need to restore to reconnect the network'. This inverts the optimization landscape and can make the search more efficient. Efficient algorithms matter because real networks are huge—millions of nodes—and exhaustive search is impossible. By using tree-like indexes to update removal strategies dynamically (when nodes are added or deleted), the method scales to real-world networks in minutes instead of hours. This lets practitioners model how targeted removal of key spreaders can disrupt misinformation cascades.

This work is an exploratory workshop agenda rather than a specific technical method. The core motivation is integrating zero-knowledge proofs (systems that prove claims without revealing the underlying data) with blockchain and post-quantum cryptography as the Web evolves toward decentralized identity and verifiable computation. The underlying principle is that decentralization requires new trust models: you cannot rely on a single authority to verify who you are or whether a computation was done correctly. Zero-knowledge proofs solve this by letting any party verify a claim directly, and post-quantum readiness ensures these proofs remain trustworthy even if quantum computers become practical. This principle applies to the emerging Internet because identity, contracts, and transactions increasingly flow through decentralized systems where no single gatekeeper exists. By gathering practitioners, standards-makers, and researchers to map failure modes and interoperability requirements, the workshop aims to guide the transition toward systems that work at scale.

The core task is explaining why protocol designers made specific choices when writing Internet standards, using language model retrieval to search years of IETF email discussions and extract the rationale buried in casual debate. The underlying principle is that retrieval-augmented generation works because the context matters: a language model can generate plausible explanations on its own, but it is much more likely to generate correct ones when given the authentic historical record to work from. Searching email archives for discussions mentioning key trade-offs (performance vs. compatibility, simplicity vs. generality) grounds the generation in what actually mattered to those designers. This principle applies because protocol standards are pragmatic documents shaped by real constraints and compromises that are not obvious from the finished text. Externalizing this reasoning from the minds of original authors and email archives makes the knowledge reusable for future learners and implementers.

The core optimization is selecting which three currency pools to arbitrage and how much to trade across them to lock in profit while respecting wallet balance, pool liquidity, and gas fees. The underlying principle is that deep reinforcement learning excels at finding high-quality solutions in a vast search space with complex constraints: the agent learns through trial and error to balance speed (can compute an answer in milliseconds) against profit (how much money it makes). Speed matters because the real blockchain only rewards the searcher whose transaction lands first. The principle applies because this is fundamentally a planning problem under time pressure: an optimal solution computed too slowly is worthless, while a quick approximate solution is profitable. By training an agent to optimize for both speed and profit together, rather than sequentially chasing profit then hunting for shortcuts, the system finds the practical Pareto frontier—the set of strategies where no better speed is possible at this profit level, and vice versa.
